title: Grand Strategic Compatibility: The Basis of The Japan-Vietnam Partnership
author: Khang Vu
text:
Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae meets with Vietnam’s President and Communist Party chief To Lam, in Hanoi, Vietnam, May. 2, 2026.
Credit: X/MOFA of Japan
In an address to Vietnam National University in Hanoi in May, Japan’s Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae affirmed Japan’s commitment to the Free and Open Indo-Pacific (FOIP) concept. Tokyo pledged to increase its political, economic, and defense cooperation with ASEAN so that each ASEAN state can “acquire autonomy and resilience” in the face of intensifying geopolitical competition. It was Takaichi’s first public address on updating her predecessor Abe Shinzo’s FOIP vision, and her decision to deliver it in Vietnam says a lot about the current state of Japan-Vietnam ties.The reconciliation between Japan and Vietnam since the end of the Cold War has been nothing short of extraordinary. During the Third Indochina War (1978-1991), Japan sided with China and the United States to isolate Vietnam due to its status as a Soviet ally. Japan’s alignment was rooted in its fear of a Soviet invasion from the north in the late 1970s. Beginning in May 1978, Moscow had increased the number of troops stationed on Soviet-controlled Southern Kuril Islands up to 6,000. The Soviets also built up their Pacific Fleet until it became the largest of the four Soviet fleets, and they deployed the SS-20 intermediate-range ballistic missiles to the Asia-Pacific theater.[...]
